title: Resource-fair quantum charging advantage
open: Can a quantum-battery charging advantage survive a fully resource-fair comparison? That is, can a scalable advantage in charging speed or work extraction be demonstrated once classical and quantum devices are matched for charger energy, interaction strength, control complexity, preparation, and readout costs?
status: Collective-charging advantages are established in models, with preliminary experiments; a broadly convincing end-to-end advantage remains outstanding. See F. Campaioli et al. (2024), *Colloquium: Quantum batteries*, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.96.031001.
solved_when: A scalable quantum charging advantage is demonstrated experimentally under matched resource budgets — equal charger energy, interaction strength, control complexity, preparation costs, and readout costs for the classical and quantum devices.
why: It determines whether quantum batteries offer genuinely useful energy technology rather than an artifact of an advantageous comparison convention.
key_works: F. Campaioli et al. (2024), *Colloquium: Quantum batteries*, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.96.031001.

title: Predictive thermal conductance of real interfaces
open: Can we predict the thermal boundary conductance of a real, manufacturable interface from its physical and chemical makeup — its chemistry, roughness, contamination, bonding, and intermixing — rather than from idealized models? That is, can a predictive theory be built that yields conductance values with uncertainty bounds that remain valid across different fabrication processes?
status: Acoustic and diffuse-mismatch models capture only limited regimes; atomistic calculations and interface-mode measurements have not produced a universal practical predictor.
solved_when: A validated predictor exists that takes as input the interface's chemistry, roughness, contamination, bonding, and intermixing, and outputs thermal boundary conductance with uncertainty bounds demonstrated to transfer across fabrication processes.
why: Interface thermal resistance is the bottleneck for electronics cooling, thermoelectrics, and high-power energy devices; a predictive capability would let these systems be designed rather than empirically tuned.
key_works: A. Giri and P. E. Hopkins (2020), *A Review of Experimental and Computational Advances in Thermal Boundary Conductance and Nanoscale Thermal Transport across Solid Interfaces*, DOI:10.1002/adfm.201903857.

title: Tight energy bounds for metal-mediated nitrogen fixation
open: What is the true minimum energy cost of producing ammonia via metal-mediated synthesis when the whole cycle is counted — regenerating the metal, recovering solvent, delivering protons, separating products, and accounting for side reactions — rather than just the idealized reduction step? Formally, determine achievable full-cycle energy bounds for such pathways.
status: A 2025 analysis (V. Azumah and V. Viswanathan, *Fundamental Limits of Dissociative Electrochemical Ammonia Synthesis via Electrodeposited Metals*, arXiv:2507.21121) derives limits for specified electrodeposited-metal pathways; broader reaction networks and practical attainability remain unresolved.
solved_when: A full-cycle minimum energy cost for metal-mediated ammonia synthesis is established with metal regeneration, solvent recovery, proton delivery, separation, and side reactions all included.
why: It identifies which catalyst improvements can actually reduce system-level energy consumption, rather than only the idealized step.
key_works: V. Azumah and V. Viswanathan (2025), *Fundamental Limits of Dissociative Electrochemical Ammonia Synthesis via Electrodeposited Metals*, arXiv:2507.21121.

title: Reversible solid-state sulfur conversion
open: Can a solid-state lithium–sulfur cell keep sulfur electrochemically reversible — maintaining both ionic and electronic contact through the conversion reaction and its volume changes — under practically acceptable conditions?
status: Solid-state lithium–sulfur architectures have been demonstrated, but practical feasibility remains governed by the simultaneous demands of mechanical stability and transport; G. Wang et al. (2025), *Assessing the practical feasibility of solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries*, DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00918-9.
solved_when: Reversible sulfur conversion is achieved without excessive stack pressure, without excessive inactive conductive additive, and without sacrificing areal capacity.
why: It would remove shuttle-related losses while preserving sulfur’s energy-density advantage, making solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries practically viable.
key_works: G. Wang et al. (2025), *Assessing the practical feasibility of solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries*, DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00918-9.

title: Reproducible aqueous nitrogen reduction
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Can nitrogen and water be converted to ammonia in an aqueous electrochemical system at a rate that is genuinely useful, in a way that survives rigorous scrutiny? A convincing demonstration would combine quantitative isotope measurements, exclusion of extraneous nitrogen contamination, full mass balances, and independent replication of the result.
status: A 2019 protocol by S. Z. Andersen et al. (*A rigorous electrochemical ammonia synthesis protocol with quantitative isotope measurements*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1260-x) addressed widespread measurement pitfalls, but analytical rigor alone does not establish a practical synthesis route.
solved_when: Aqueous electrochemical ammonia production is demonstrated with quantitative isotope verification of the nitrogen source, contamination controls, complete material balances, and independent replication by a separate group.
why: It cleanly distinguishes true nitrogen fixation from trace-contamination artifacts, which is the central credibility barrier in this field.
key_works: S. Z. Andersen et al. (2019), *A rigorous electrochemical ammonia synthesis protocol with quantitative isotope measurements*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1260-x.

title: Grid-forming recovery after current saturation
open: How can a grid-forming converter be made to return predictably from current-limited fault operation to normal grid-forming behavior, without losing synchronization or triggering damaging secondary transients? Formally, the goal is a converter control design whose recovery trajectory from saturated operation provably remains synchronized and transient-bounded.
status: Current limitation is necessary for semiconductor protection, but its interaction with grid-forming dynamics remains a central open control problem (see Lin et al. (2020), grid-forming inverter roadmap, NREL/TP-5D00-73476); related directions include stability of saturated hybrid controllers and basin-of-attraction estimation.
solved_when: A converter design demonstrates recovery from current-limited fault operation back to normal grid-forming behavior that is predictable in the sense of preserving synchronization and avoiding damaging secondary transients; in the absence of stated quantitative budgets, a validated design meeting these qualitative criteria (e.g., by analysis or Hardware-in-the-Loop/field demonstration) suffices.
why: Fault survival requires more than avoiding immediate device destruction — a converter that survives the fault but recovers unpredictably can still destabilize or damage the grid it is meant to form.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), grid-forming inverter roadmap, NREL/TP-5D00-73476.

title: Convergence of all-orders near-axis expansions
open: Do stellarator near-axis expansions actually converge? Establish convergence radii or useful remainder bounds for these expansions — including at finite pressure — rather than merely generating formal coefficients to arbitrary order.
status: An all-orders axis-expansion framework was developed in 2024 (W. Sengupta et al., *Stellarator equilibrium axis-expansion to all orders in distance from the axis for arbitrary plasma beta*, arXiv:2402.17034; DOI:10.1017/S002237782400076X). Formal solvability, however, does not establish convergence at the finite minor radius needed by an actual device.
solved_when: A convergence radius or explicit remainder bound is proved for the near-axis expansion, sufficient to certify the approximation at the finite minor radius of an actual device, with finite plasma pressure included.
why: It converts a powerful design construction into a quantitatively certified approximation usable in real stellarator design.
key_works: W. Sengupta et al. (2024), *Stellarator equilibrium axis-expansion to all orders in distance from the axis for arbitrary plasma beta*, arXiv:2402.17034; DOI:10.1017/S002237782400076X.

title: A physically calibrated quasisymmetry-error metric
open: Can we define a quasisymmetry-error measure that is both computable and physically meaningful, so that a smaller value reliably means better confinement? Formally, the measure should come with bounds on transport or particle-loss observables across energy, pitch angle, collisionality, and equilibrium variation.
status: Existing measures need not rank configurations consistently: the 2022 comparison of quasisymmetry measures (E. Rodríguez, E. J. Paul, and A. Bhattacharjee, *Measures of quasisymmetry for stellarators*, arXiv:2109.13080; DOI:10.1017/S0022377821001331) demonstrates why minimizing a convenient geometric norm is not equivalent to minimizing every physical loss.
solved_when: A computable quasisymmetry-error metric exists together with provable bounds on relevant transport or particle-loss observables that hold across energy, pitch angle, collisionality, and equilibrium variation.
why: Without such a metric, stellarator optimization can improve a geometric surrogate while actually worsening confinement, wasting effort on configurations that are better only on paper.
key_works: E. Rodríguez, E. J. Paul, and A. Bhattacharjee (2022), *Measures of quasisymmetry for stellarators*, arXiv:2109.13080; DOI:10.1017/S0022377821001331.

title: Collisional boundary layers in piecewise-omnigenous fields
open: What transport actually arises near the boundaries between differently trapped orbit classes in piecewise-omnigenous fields? In particular, determine this transport in the presence of collisions, finite orbit width, and realistic smoothing of the idealized geometry.
status: Piecewise omnigenity was introduced in 2024 (J. L. Velasco et al., *Piecewise omnigenous stellarators*, arXiv:2405.07634; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.185101) with favorable transport properties. The construction does not eliminate the need to resolve transitions between orbit regions.
solved_when: A quantified account of boundary-layer transport between orbit regions is obtained that includes collisions, finite orbit width, and realistic smoothing of idealized geometry, resolving the transitions between orbit regions left unaddressed by the construction.
why: It tests whether this larger, more manufacturable confinement family retains its apparent transport advantage once the unresolved transitions between orbit regions are accounted for.
key_works: J. L. Velasco et al. (2024), *Piecewise omnigenous stellarators*, arXiv:2405.07634; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.185101.

title: Predicting pedestal density without prescribing it
open: Can the pedestal density and temperature profiles be predicted jointly from first-principles physics — fueling, recycling, neutral penetration, turbulence, and stability — rather than supplied as an external input to a pedestal-height model? In formal terms, this asks for a closed, self-consistent prediction of the full pedestal state in which particle balance is solved alongside the stability constraints that currently set pedestal height and width.
status: EPED established a successful stability-based framework for predicting pedestal height and width (P. B. Snyder et al., 2011, *A first-principles predictive model of the pedestal height and width: development, testing and ITER optimization with the EPED model*), but it takes density as given; a closed prediction of particle balance and the entire pedestal state remains open and is a stronger requirement.
solved_when: A predictive model exists that outputs pedestal density and temperature profiles directly from fueling, recycling, neutral penetration, turbulence, and stability inputs, with no externally prescribed density, and whose predictions are validated in the manner EPED-style pedestal-height models have been tested.
why: Density assumptions strongly affect predicted fusion performance and operating margins, so an assumed rather than predicted pedestal density can bias reactor projections and the operating space derived from them.
key_works: P. B. Snyder et al. (2011), *A first-principles predictive model of the pedestal height and width: development, testing and ITER optimization with the EPED model*.

title: Predictive isotope scaling of core heat transport
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how swapping hydrogen isotopes changes heat transport in a tokamak core, when heating deposition, density profiles, rotation, and impurity content are independently controlled? In formal terms, is there a validated, transferable isotope-scaling law for core heat transport that accounts for the coupled changes these controls induce?
status: A 2025 JET study combines deuterium–tritium comparisons with gyrokinetic simulations, but its agreement for selected discharges does not establish a transferable isotope-scaling law.
solved_when: A predictive scaling law or validated theoretical framework exists that reproduces and forecasts isotope-dependent changes in core heat transport across discharges, not just selected cases, with the effects of heating deposition, density profiles, rotation, and impurity content independently controlled.
why: It directly reduces uncertainty in extrapolating heat transport measured in nontritium experiments to deuterium–tritium burning plasmas, where no direct experimental tuning is possible.
key_works: JET Contributors (2025), *Experimental study and gyrokinetic simulations of isotope effects on core heat transport in JET tokamak deuterium and tritium plasmas*, DOI:10.1088/1741-4326/adab04.

title: Reactor-relevant impurity seeding in negative triangularity
open: Can a negative-triangularity tokamak plasma radiate a large fraction of its input power using reactor-relevant seeded impurities while still maintaining favorable confinement and particle exhaust, and without those impurities accumulating unacceptably in the core?
status: Highly radiating negative-triangularity plasmas have been demonstrated (L. Casali et al., 2025, *Achievement of highly radiating plasmas in negative triangularity and effect of reactor-relevant seeded impurities on confinement and transport*); the remaining gap is a transferable operating window with self-consistent impurity transport. For background on negative-triangularity tokamak plasmas, see A. Marinoni, O. Sauter, and S. Coda (2021), *A brief history of negative triangularity tokamak plasmas*.
solved_when: A transferable operating window is demonstrated in negative triangularity in which highly radiating, reactor-relevant impurity-seeded plasmas retain favorable confinement and particle exhaust with no unacceptable core impurity accumulation, with impurity transport treated self-consistently.
why: A confinement configuration must also solve its exhaust problem: without a compatible exhaust solution, negative triangularity cannot serve as a reactor concept regardless of its confinement benefits.
key_works: L. Casali et al. (2025), *Achievement of highly radiating plasmas in negative triangularity and effect of reactor-relevant seeded impurities on confinement and transport*; A. Marinoni, O. Sauter, and S. Coda (2021), *A brief history of negative triangularity tokamak plasmas*.

title: Reactor-scale scrape-off-layer heat-width prediction
open: Can we predict how wide the divertor heat-flux channel will be in reactor-scale tokamaks, given that present-day devices sit on the small side of the relevant scale transition? A successful theory would reconcile the roles of magnetic drifts, turbulence, and machine size into an extrapolable prediction across that regime change.
status: Heuristic scaling arguments, notably Goldston's 2012 heuristic drift-based model for the power scrape-off width in low-gas-puff H-mode tokamaks, and large kinetic simulations — including PPPL's 2021 XGC reactor-scale divertor-heat-load simulations — provide different forms of evidence. A validated extrapolation across the relevant regime change remains necessary.
solved_when: A validated prediction of the scrape-off-layer heat-flux width across the transition from present devices to reactor-scale plasmas exists, with the competing contributions of magnetic drifts, turbulence, and machine size resolved.
why: Small errors in the predicted heat width translate into large errors in component heat loading, so divertor design in reactors hinges directly on this prediction.
key_works: R. J. Goldston (2012), *Heuristic drift-based model of the power scrape-off width in low-gas-puff H-mode tokamaks*; PPPL (2021), research account of XGC reactor-scale divertor-heat-load simulations.

title: Nonlocal parallel heat-flux closure without tuning
open: Can reduced, closure-based models reproduce kinetic parallel heat transport across steep, evolving edge gradients without any discharge-specific tuning, replacing the empirical flux limiters currently in use? Formally, is there a nonlocal parallel heat-flux closure that matches kinetic solutions over rapidly changing collisionality regimes using only first-principles parameters?
status: Nonlocal kernels and kinetic comparisons were developed in 2018 (G. Ciraolo et al., 2018, *Fluid and kinetic modelling for non-local heat transport in magnetic fusion devices*, arXiv:1801.01177; DOI:10.1002/ctpp.201700222), and subsequent scrape-off-layer studies have incorporated nonlocal transport; general accuracy across rapidly changing collisionality remains unresolved.
solved_when: A reduced closure reproduces kinetic parallel heat transport through steep, evolving edge gradients with general accuracy across rapidly changing collisionality, with no discharge-specific tuning parameters.
why: It would improve predictions of detachment, transient heat loads, and target temperatures in magnetic fusion edge plasmas, where flux-limited fluid models are currently relied upon.
key_works: G. Ciraolo et al. (2018), *Fluid and kinetic modelling for non-local heat transport in magnetic fusion devices*, arXiv:1801.01177; DOI:10.1002/ctpp.201700222.

title: Error-controlled switching between runaway-electron models
open: Can we build a hybrid simulation of runaway-electron generation that shifts between a reduced description and a full kinetic description on the fly, without discarding the kinetic memory accumulated so far, and with a certified bound on the error it introduces in the predicted seed population?
status: Olasz et al. (2021) identified a collision-timescale criterion for the failure of quasi-stationary Dreicer approximations in dynamic scenarios (arXiv:2101.02740; DOI:10.1088/1741-4326/abf0de). A complete error-controlled switching scheme, which is a stronger requirement, has not been achieved.
solved_when: An adaptive switching scheme exists that preserves the evolving electron distribution across model transitions and carries a provable error bound on predicted seed populations.
why: It would let integrated disruption simulations run at reduced-model cost while guaranteeing that essential kinetic memory is not silently lost — the failure mode that currently makes cheap simulations untrustworthy.
key_works: S. Olasz et al. (2021), *Validity of models for Dreicer generation of runaway electrons in dynamic scenarios*, arXiv:2101.02740; DOI:10.1088/1741-4326/abf0de.

title: Tritium inventory from evolving tungsten defect populations
open: Can we predict how much tritium a tungsten plasma-facing component retains when its trapping landscape — irradiation defects, helium bubbles, grain boundaries, and surface deposits — is itself evolving during service rather than fixed? The goal is a predictive model of retained tritium under simultaneous neutron, thermal, and plasma exposure with dynamically changing trap populations.
status: Laboratory retention studies identify strong material-history effects, but extrapolating those measurements to simultaneous neutron, thermal, and plasma exposure remains unresolved. Key works: E. Bernard et al. (2019), *Tritium retention in W plasma-facing materials: Impact of…* — full subtitle **(verify)**, Nuclear Materials and Energy, article PII:S2352179118302424.
solved_when: A validated method exists that infers and predicts retained tritium inventory in tungsten whose defect populations evolve during service, and whose predictions are shown to extrapolate laboratory retention measurements to simultaneous neutron, thermal, and plasma exposure.
why: It links material degradation directly to recoverable fuel inventory and to how fusion components can be handled, reused, or disposed of after service.
key_works: E. Bernard et al. (2019), *Tritium retention in W plasma-facing materials: Impact of…* — full subtitle **(verify)**, Nuclear Materials and Energy, article PII:S2352179118302424.

title: Spatiotemporal mix reconstruction from radiochemical products
open: Can we reconstruct when, where, and in what amount ablator material mixed with fuel during an inertial confinement fusion implosion, using radiochemical products together with other diagnostics, while quantifying how nonunique the reconstruction is?
status: A 2025 study measured technetium–molybdenum isotope ratios across a NIF campaign (K. N. Kmak et al. (2025), *Using radiochemistry to diagnose fuel-ablator mix in inertial confinement fusion studies at the National Ignition Facility…*, DOI:10.3389/fchem.2025.1632948). Integrated product yields constrain mix but do not uniquely reconstruct its complete history.
solved_when: A reconstruction of the spatiotemporal mix history is obtained that recovers timing, location, and magnitude of fuel–ablator mixing from radiochemical products combined with other diagnostics, with an accompanying quantification of the nonuniqueness of the solution.
why: It distinguishes different failure mechanisms that produce similar final yields, turning endpoint measurements into mechanism-specific diagnosis.
key_works: K. N. Kmak et al. (2025), *Using radiochemistry to diagnose fuel-ablator mix in inertial confinement fusion studies at the National Ignition Facility…*, DOI:10.3389/fchem.2025.1632948.

title: Where the solid-electrolyte interphase actually grows
open: Where in a heterogeneous solid-electrolyte interphase do the reactions that grow it actually occur, and how do the growth fronts move as electrolyte composition, electrode potential, and interphase age change? Formally, the goal is to map the reaction-location distribution within the interphase and track its moving growth fronts across these variables.
status: Isotope-assisted depth profiling demonstrated bottom-up growth in a studied system in 2018 (Z. Liu et al., *A Bottom-Up Formation Mechanism of Solid Electrolyte Interphase Revealed by Isotope-Assisted Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry*, DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.8b02350). That single mechanism should not be assumed universal across chemistries and cycling histories.
solved_when: Reaction locations and moving growth fronts within the interphase are determined as a function of electrolyte composition, electrode potential, and age, without assuming a single mechanism is universal across chemistries and cycling histories.
why: The growth location determines which species must transport across the interphase, and therefore dictates how passivation of the electrode can be improved.
key_works: Z. Liu et al. (2018), *A Bottom-Up Formation Mechanism of Solid Electrolyte Interphase Revealed by Isotope-Assisted Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry*, DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.8b02350.

title: Separating calendar corrosion from cycling-induced lithium loss
open: How much lithium is consumed while an anode simply sits at rest, separately from what is lost during plating and stripping, and how does that loss depend on the state of charge and on the morphology left behind by earlier cycling?
status: In-situ NMR has resolved both dead-lithium formation and corrosion (Gunnarsdóttir et al. 2020, PMCID:PMC7729915). Going beyond identifying both mechanisms to a transferable model for arbitrary rest–cycle histories remains more demanding.
solved_when: A quantitative, transferable account of rest-time lithium consumption is available that decouples corrosion from deposition and stripping losses and predicts the effect of state of charge and prior morphology across arbitrary rest–cycle histories.
why: A cell can cycle with high efficiency yet still fail on the shelf, so separating these degradation clocks is needed to predict and improve calendar life.
key_works: Gunnarsdóttir et al. (2020), *Noninvasive In Situ NMR Study of “Dead Lithium” Formation and Lithium Corrosion in Full-Cell Lithium Metal Batteries*, PMCID:PMC7729915.

title: Enumerating stable states of lossy grids with realistic controls
open: Can the topology-based enumeration of synchronous operating states be extended to power grid models that include voltage dynamics, reactive-power limits, converter controls, and protection transitions — that is, to realistic lossy networks beyond the idealized oscillator setting? A complete answer would give a method to enumerate the stable states of such models based on network structure rather than repeated simulation.
status: Delabays, Jafarpour, and Bullo showed how winding partitions organize multiple synchronous states in lossy oscillator models, and their analysis shows that dissipation can increase multistability [R. Delabays, S. Jafarpour, and F. Bullo (2022), *Multistability and anomalies in oscillator models of lossy power grids*, arXiv:2202.02439; DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32931-8].
solved_when: A topology-based enumeration procedure exists for networks incorporating voltage dynamics, reactive-power limits, converter controls, and protection transitions, and its results can be checked against the stable states of those models.
why: It would reveal stable but undesirable operating states that a single initialization of the grid model would miss.
key_works: R. Delabays, S. Jafarpour, and F. Bullo (2022), *Multistability and anomalies in oscillator models of lossy power grids*, arXiv:2202.02439; DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32931-8.

title: Elimination or certification of spurious state-estimation minima
open: When does a nonlinear state-estimation problem admit misleading local minima, and can we build estimators that either avoid these spurious solutions or certify that a returned estimate is globally adequate?
status: Spurious local minima have been studied explicitly, notably in R. Y. Zhang and J. Lavaei (2019), *Spurious Local Minima in Power System State Estimation*. Known convexity or benign-landscape results hold only for restricted formulations and do not extend to every measurement layout.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the measurement layouts (or problem structure) under which spurious local minima do or do not occur, together with an algorithm that provably avoids them or certifies global adequacy of its output.
why: A numerically converged estimate can still be physically wrong, so operators of estimation-heavy systems cannot currently trust local convergence as evidence of correctness.
key_works: R. Y. Zhang and J. Lavaei (2019), *Spurious Local Minima in Power System State Estimation*.

title: Braess-safe network reinforcement
open: Which network additions or capacity upgrades can be guaranteed not to worsen specified congestion or stability metrics over a defined uncertainty set — and conversely, under what conditions must every intervention carry some risk of worsening them?
status: Braess-type worsening in power grids has been analyzed and demonstrated in models (B. Schäfer et al. (2022), *Understanding Braess' paradox in power grids*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32917-6). The existence of the paradox is solved context; safe intervention selection remains open.
solved_when: A characterization exists of interventions (new links or capacity upgrades) that provably never worsen the chosen congestion or stability metrics over the stated uncertainty set, or a proof that such guarantees are impossible for given network classes and metrics.
why: Because of Braess-type paradoxes, adding infrastructure can degrade network performance, so planners currently lack a principled way to certify that an upgrade is actually safe.
key_works: B. Schäfer et al. (2022), *Understanding Braess’ paradox in power grids*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32917-6.

title: Atomic identity of LeTID-active defect complexes
open: What defect complexes and charge-state transitions actually cause light- and elevated-temperature-induced degradation (LeTID) in silicon? A complete answer would uniquely identify the microscopic defect complexes responsible across the relevant silicon materials and processing histories, rather than merely fitting their kinetic signatures.
status: Hydrogen-based explanations, notably D. Chen et al. (2020), *Hydrogen-induced degradation: Explaining the mechanism behind light- and elevated temperature-induced degradation in n- and p-type silicon*, DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2019.110353, reproduce important observations; however, reproducing degradation kinetics is not equivalent to uniquely identifying the microscopic defect, and kinetic-model nonuniqueness and reliance on indirect spectroscopy remain obstacles.
solved_when: The LeTID-active defect complex(es) and their charge-state transitions are uniquely identified at the atomic scale, across relevant silicon materials and processing histories, and shown to account for the observed degradation kinetics.
why: With the defect known, degradation can be prevented by targeted materials or process design, replacing empirical process recipes that work without understood causes.
key_works: D. Chen et al. (2020), *Hydrogen-induced degradation: Explaining the mechanism behind light- and elevated temperature-induced degradation in n- and p-type silicon*, DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2019.110353.

title: Energy-selective contacts without excessive heat leakage
open: Can hot-carrier solar cells be equipped with energy-selective contacts that extract carriers over a narrow energy window while maintaining enough electrical conductance and without leaking heat back into the absorber?
status: Analyses of nonideal contacts (A. S. Sharma et al. (2023), *Heat Flow through Nonideal Contacts in Hot-Carrier Solar Cells*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevApplied.20.034001) quantify how heat flow through real contacts undermines hot-carrier conversion, but the perfectly selective contacts treated in models do not correspond to a realizable device.
solved_when: An experimentally realizable contact structure demonstrates both narrow energy-selective extraction and useful electrical conductance in an actual device, with parasitic heat exchange suppressed to levels that do not undermine hot-carrier conversion.
why: Slow carrier cooling in the absorber is useless unless a compatible extraction mechanism exists; energy-selective contacts are the missing link between hot-carrier absorption and usable electrical work.
key_works: A. S. Sharma et al. (2023), *Heat Flow through Nonideal Contacts in Hot-Carrier Solar Cells*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevApplied.20.034001.

title: Perovskite reverse-bias survival under realistic shading
open: Can a perovskite solar module survive the reverse biases that module-level shading inevitably imposes on individual cells — including repeated events and realistic protection circuitry — without irreversible local damage?
status: Improved reverse-bias stability has been demonstrated through contact and electrode design (F. Jiang et al. (2024), *Improved reverse bias stability in p–i–n perovskite solar cells with optimized hole transport materials and less reactive electrodes*, Nature Energy 9, 1275–1284). That does not establish lifetime survival across module fault and shading histories.
solved_when: A module design demonstrates survival under realistic shading and fault histories, with protection circuitry, over repeated reverse-bias events and the module lifetime, without irreversible local damage.
why: Ordinary outdoor shading must not become a destructive electrochemical event.
key_works: F. Jiang et al. (2024), *Improved reverse bias stability in p–i–n perovskite solar cells with optimized hole transport materials and less reactive electrodes*, Nature Energy 9, 1275–1284.

title: Persistent permeability beyond conventional brittle behavior
open: Can connected flow paths created in superhot rock stay useful over prolonged circulation? The goal is to demonstrate permeability that persists under the temperatures, stresses, and chemical conditions expected during long-term operation.
status: Watanabe et al. demonstrated cloud-fracture networks in high-temperature experiments (N. Watanabe et al. (2019), *Cloud-fracture networks as a means of accessing superhot geothermal energy*, PMCID:PMC6353971), but initial permeability creation does not establish long-duration reservoir performance.
solved_when: Connected flow paths are created in superhot rock and shown to remain functional under the expected thermal, stress, and chemical conditions over prolonged circulation — not merely at initial creation.
why: It determines whether accessible superhot rock can serve as a usable heat exchanger; initial permeability creation alone does not establish a long-duration reservoir.
key_works: N. Watanabe et al. (2019), *Cloud-fracture networks as a means of accessing superhot geothermal energy*, PMCID:PMC6353971.

title: Freeze-plug actuation across the full reactor operating history
open: Can a freeze plug — a solidified salt seal in a drain line — be shown to thaw and open the drain path passively, purely from loss of active cooling, regardless of the reactor's thermal history beforehand?
status: A 2019 study of the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (M. Tiberga et al., *Preliminary investigation on the melting behavior of a freeze-valve for the Molten Salt Fast Reactor*) shows that thawing behavior depends strongly on geometry and available heating, so passive actuation cannot be assumed from the material's melting temperature alone.
solved_when: Reliable passive thawing and drainage following loss of active cooling is demonstrated across low-power, startup, shutdown, and nominal-power operating histories.
why: A freeze-plug shutdown mechanism is only credible if it actuates when the preceding operating state is unfavorable; otherwise the core's passive safety claim fails exactly when it matters.
key_works: M. Tiberga et al. (2019), *Preliminary investigation on the melting behavior of a freeze-valve for the Molten Salt Fast Reactor*.

title: Maintaining the protective oxygen window in lead coolants
open: Can oxygen activity be controlled throughout an entire lead or lead–bismuth coolant circuit so that protective surface layers persist on all components without excessive oxide precipitation — including in cold regions, during transients, and as material inventories change?
status: Oxygen management is an established corrosion-control strategy. The 2022 materials assessment documents competing dissolution, oxidation, and precipitation processes that prevent one nominal bulk oxygen concentration from guaranteeing protection everywhere (X. Gong et al. (2022), *Environmental degradation of structural materials in liquid lead- and lead-bismuth eutectic-cooled reactors*, DOI:10.1016/j.pmatsci.2022.100920).
solved_when: A control strategy maintains oxygen activity such that protective oxide layers persist everywhere in the circuit, including cold regions, under transients and changing material inventories, while avoiding excessive oxide precipitation.
why: A chemistry setting that protects one component can foul or damage another, so circuit-wide oxygen control is what makes lead-cooled systems operationally viable.
key_works: X. Gong et al. (2022), *Environmental degradation of structural materials in liquid lead- and lead-bismuth eutectic-cooled reactors*, DOI:10.1016/j.pmatsci.2022.100920.

title: Long-horizon effects of intermittent water ingress in pitch bearings
open: Does a pitch bearing that appears to recover after a water-ingress episode actually recover, or does repeated contamination, drying, grease replacement, and load variation leave latent damage that accelerates later wear? The challenge is to predict damage over a long horizon of such intermittent episodes rather than treating water content as a fixed test parameter.
status: Short-term pitch-bearing water-ingress experiments were reported in 2024 (M. Stammler et al., Lubricants 12, 310, DOI:10.3390/lubricants12090310), but they do not determine whether apparently recoverable contamination leaves latent damage that accelerates later wear.
solved_when: A predictive account exists of how repeated cycles of water contamination, drying, lubricant replacement, and changing loads accumulate damage over the bearing's service life, and it determines whether apparently recoverable contamination leaves latent damage that accelerates later wear.
why: Maintenance decisions depend on whether removing contaminated grease restores the bearing or merely hides continuing damage; knowing this determines when intervention is genuinely preventive versus cosmetic.
key_works: M. Stammler et al. (2024), pitch-bearing water-ingress study, Lubricants 12, 310, DOI:10.3390/lubricants12090310.

title: Field-calibrated fatigue prediction for large roller pitch bearings
open: Can rolling-contact fatigue predictions for large roller pitch bearings be validated against representative service histories, accounting for ring deformation, manufacturing variation, lubrication, and nonuniform roller loading?
status: Menck, Schleich, and Stammler developed detailed fatigue calculations for a three-row roller pitch bearing in a wind turbine in 2025 (DOI:10.5194/wes-10-2771-2025); however, numerical stress resolution does not itself validate accumulated lifetime damage.
solved_when: A fatigue calculation for a large roller pitch bearing is checked against service data that captures ring deformation, manufacturing variation, lubrication, and nonuniform roller loading, so that accumulated lifetime damage — not just numerical stress resolution — is confirmed.
why: Accurate contact mechanics must translate into credible failure probabilities and replacement intervals.
key_works: O. Menck, F. Schleich, and M. Stammler (2025), *Rolling contact fatigue calculation of a three-row roller pitch bearing in a wind turbine*, DOI:10.5194/wes-10-2771-2025.

title: Long-lived oxygen-tolerant electrochemical carbon capture
open: Can an electrochemical carbon capture system hold its capture capacity and efficiency when fed oxygen-containing gas continuously over a long campaign, rather than only surviving short oxygen exposure? In particular, how does it behave under variable water content and as trace reaction products accumulate in the electrolyte?
status: Abdinejad and colleagues demonstrated an oxygen-stable redox-active capture chemistry in 2024 (M. Abdinejad et al., *Oxygen-Stable Electrochemical CO2 Capture using Redox-Active Heterocyclic Benzodithiophene Quinone*, DOI:10.1002/anie.202412229). Oxygen tolerance in a selected experiment is not equivalent to complete long-term electrolyte stability, so long-campaign durability remains unestablished.
solved_when: A capture medium demonstrates sustained capture capacity and electrochemical efficiency over a long-duration campaign in oxygen-containing feed, including under water variability and accumulation of trace reaction products.
why: Avoiding the costly step of oxygen removal from feed gas is valuable only if the capture medium survives direct, prolonged oxygen exposure; otherwise the savings are illusory.
key_works: M. Abdinejad et al. (2024), *Oxygen-Stable Electrochemical CO2 Capture using Redox-Active Heterocyclic Benzodithiophene Quinone*, DOI:10.1002/anie.202412229.

title: Transferable annual algal-productivity forecasts
open: Can we predict the annual recoverable biomass of an algal cultivation site before it is built or replanted? The aim is a forecasting framework that transfers across sites and incorporates weather, strain selection, crop rotation, harvesting, contamination, and downtime — rather than extrapolating from peak seasonal growth rates.
status: The current state of the art is empirical rather than predictive: McGowen and colleagues demonstrated annual productivity improvements through crop rotation and operational management in 2023 (J. McGowen et al. (2023), *Outdoor annual algae productivity improvements at the pre-pilot scale through crop rotation and pond operational management strategies*, DOI:10.1016/j.algal.2023.102995).
solved_when: A predictive model exists that estimates annual recoverable biomass at sites beyond those used to calibrate it, explicitly accounting for weather, strain selection, crop rotation, harvesting, contamination, and downtime, with accuracy validated across multiple environments rather than single-site seasonal fits.
why: Fuel and bioproduct economics hinge on total annual output from the complete cultivation system, not on peak-season growth; a transferable forecast would let operators and investors judge site viability before committing capital.
key_works: J. McGowen et al. (2023), *Outdoor annual algae productivity improvements at the pre-pilot scale through crop rotation and pond operational management strategies*, DOI:10.1016/j.algal.2023.102995.

title: High boron rejection without excessive desalination penalties
open: Can a membrane reject neutral boron species at realistic seawater feed conditions while preserving water permeability, membrane stability, and acceptable pressure or chemical-adjustment requirements?
status: Huang and colleagues improved boron rejection and permeability in 2025 using tailored thin-film nanocomposite membranes (g-C₃N₄-tuned diffusion and reaction, DOI:10.1016/j.desal.2025.118902). Promising coupons do not establish durable module performance in real seawater.
solved_when: A membrane demonstrates high rejection of neutral boron at relevant feed conditions while maintaining water permeability and membrane stability without excessive pressure increase or chemical pretreatment, ideally validated beyond coupon scale in real seawater.
why: Meeting boron specifications otherwise forces additional treatment stages that increase energy consumption and process complexity, so a single-pass solution would directly cut desalination cost and energy.
key_works: J. Huang et al. (2025), *Enhanced boron rejection and permeability of thin-film nanocomposite membranes via g-C₃N₄-tuned diffusion and reaction*, DOI:10.1016/j.desal.2025.118902.

title: Whole-cycle validation of ultrasonic water extraction
open: Does the energy saved at the extraction stage survive the rest of the device? Specifically, determine whether ultrasonic extraction lowers the complete-system energy per unit of usable water once capture, airflow, electronics, and recovery are all included, not just the extraction step alone.
status: Shuvo and colleagues reported a large extraction-stage energy improvement in 2025 (I. I. Shuvo et al., *High-efficiency atmospheric water harvesting enabled by ultrasonic extraction*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65586-2). That comparison should not be interpreted as the same improvement in every component or in total water-production energy.
solved_when: A whole-cycle measurement shows the reduced extraction energy yields lower total device energy per unit of usable water, with capture, airflow, electronics, and recovery accounted for.
why: Component-level advantages can be diluted or even reversed by the energy demands of the rest of the device, so the headline gain may not translate into real water-production savings.
key_works: I. I. Shuvo et al. (2025), *High-efficiency atmospheric water harvesting enabled by ultrasonic extraction*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65586-2.

title: Scalable synthesis of genuinely ordered bulk tetrataenite
open: Can bulk tetrataenite — the ordered L1₀ phase of FeNi — be synthesized at scale, in substantial quantities, at practical processing times and temperatures, with ordering verified independently rather than inferred from diffraction features that could come from other phases?
status: A prominent 2022 bulk-casting claim was reinterpreted and retracted. 2025 work (S. R. Maness, S. M. Pennell, and D. C. Dunand, *Investigating the effect of phosphorus on L1₀ ordering in melt-solidified Fe-Ni alloys*, DOI:10.1016/j.mtla.2025.102617) re-examines phosphorus-assisted ordering, but the corrected evidence does not establish that phosphorus alone solves rapid bulk production.
solved_when: Substantial quantities of genuinely ordered L1₀ FeNi are produced at practical processing times and temperatures, with independent verification of the ordering (not diffraction features attributable to other phases).
why: Tetrataenite is attractive as a permanent-magnet material only if its ordered phase can be manufactured reliably rather than obtained through geological timescales or ambiguous measurements.
key_works: S. R. Maness, S. M. Pennell, and D. C. Dunand (2025), *Investigating the effect of phosphorus on L1₀ ordering in melt-solidified Fe-Ni alloys*, DOI:10.1016/j.mtla.2025.102617.

title: Tetrataenite microstructures with useful permanent-magnet coercivity
open: Can tetrataenite be processed into bulk microstructures — combining chemical ordering with controlled grain size, texture, defects, and domain structure — that deliver genuinely useful permanent-magnet coercivity and energy product?
status: Houghton and colleagues emphasize that identifying an ordered phase is not equivalent to producing an effective permanent magnet; a suitable magnetic microstructure remains an additional requirement (O. S. Houghton et al. (2025), *Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings*, DOI:10.1002/advs.202408796).
solved_when: A bulk-scale tetrataenite material is demonstrated whose chemical ordering, grain size, texture, defects, and domain structure together produce useful coercivity and energy product.
why: A material can possess favorable intrinsic anisotropy while remaining a poor practical magnet; the microstructure is what turns the intrinsic physics into a usable magnet.
key_works: O. S. Houghton et al. (2025), *Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings*, DOI:10.1002/advs.202408796.

title: Electrolyte removal without damaging recyclable graphite
open: Can electrolyte residues and their decomposition products be removed from spent lithium-ion battery graphite without degrading the graphite's recyclable properties? The target is a process that preserves graphite quality while minimizing solvent consumption, thermal treatment, and secondary emissions.
status: Rothermel and colleagues compared graphite-recycling approaches, including carbon-dioxide-assisted extraction, in 2016. A method effective for one returned-cell stream may not tolerate different binders and electrolyte histories.
solved_when: A removal method exists that cleans electrolyte residues and decomposition products from returned-cell graphite while preserving graphite properties and holding solvent use, thermal treatment, and secondary emissions to a minimum.
why: Purification can destroy part of the material value that recycling is intended to preserve, undermining the economics and environmental benefit of graphite recovery.
key_works: S. Rothermel et al. (2016), *Graphite Recycling from Spent Lithium-Ion Batteries*, DOI:10.1002/cssc.201601062.

title: Predicting strontium-vanadate cathode burn-in
open: Can the time-dependent emitting state of SrVO₃ be predicted from temperature, oxygen activity, surface termination, and prior operation — and can preparation conditions be found that reliably produce stable emission? Formally, this is a predictive model linking environmental and processing history to the evolving surface state and its emission behavior.
status: Experiments published in 2024 document substantial changes in emission during extended heating, associated with evolving surface composition. Initial work-function measurements therefore do not establish operating performance. Key work: M. S. Sheikh et al. (2024), *Time dependence of SrVO3 thermionic electron emission properties*, DOI:10.1063/5.0186012.
solved_when: A quantitative prediction of emission evolution under specified conditions is validated against experiment, and a set of preparation conditions is demonstrated to reproducibly yield stable emission over extended heating.
why: A reproducible low-work-function material is useful only if its favorable surface survives and can be manufactured consistently; without this, initial work-function measurements cannot establish operating performance.
key_works: M. S. Sheikh et al. (2024), *Time dependence of SrVO3 thermionic electron emission properties*, DOI:10.1063/5.0186012.

title: Transferring near-unity quantum yield into the visible spectrum
open: Can overall water splitting achieve near-unity quantum yields under visible light, matching what has been demonstrated in the ultraviolet? Formally, this means simultaneous stoichiometric H₂/O₂ production, stable catalytic operation, and useful solar-to-hydrogen efficiency under visible photons.
status: Takata and colleagues reported approximately 96% apparent quantum yield at 350–365 nm in 2020 (T. Takata et al., *Photocatalytic water splitting with a quantum efficiency of almost unity*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2278-9). That ultraviolet result is not 96% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency and does not establish equivalent visible-light performance.
solved_when: Overall water splitting under visible illumination retains stoichiometric gas production and catalyst stability while delivering useful solar-to-hydrogen efficiency, with per-photon efficiency approaching the approximately 96% apparent quantum yield demonstrated at 350–365 nm in the ultraviolet.
why: Solar usefulness depends on the captured spectrum as well as the efficiency of individual absorbed photons; a UV-only champion material cannot drive practical solar hydrogen production.
key_works: T. Takata et al. (2020), *Photocatalytic water splitting with a quantum efficiency of almost unity*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2278-9.

title: Simultaneous high efficiency and decade-scale PEC lifetime
open: Can a photoelectrochemical water-splitting device reach DOE's historical ultimate target of 25% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency while also operating for ten years before its output falls to 80% of the initial value?
status: These are historical program targets, not a newly issued standard or an achieved combined result. High-efficiency demonstrations, including a 19% monolithic device (W. H. Cheng et al., 2018, *Monolithic photoelectrochemical device for direct water splitting with 19% efficiency*), do not establish decade-scale qualification.
solved_when: A device is demonstrated with both 25% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency and ten years of operation before output degrades to 80% of its initial value.
why: Efficiency and lifetime jointly determine whether semiconductor-intensive direct solar hydrogen is economical, so neither alone suffices to establish viability.
key_works: DOE, *Technical Targets for Hydrogen Production: Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting*; W. H. Cheng et al. (2018), *Monolithic photoelectrochemical device for direct water splitting with 19% efficiency*.

title: Low-loss ion separation in a closed ionocaloric refrigerator
open: Can the work required to separate and regenerate the working mixture after ion-induced melting be substantially reduced without sacrificing cooling rate, temperature lift, or cycle efficiency?
status: Lilley and Prasher demonstrated an ionocaloric refrigeration cycle in 2022 (DOI:10.1126/science.ade1696). The existence of the cycle is established; competitive, durable separation and regeneration at useful scale remain the engineering target.
solved_when: A closed ionocaloric refrigerator demonstrates separation and regeneration at a useful scale with low separation work while preserving the cooling rate, temperature lift, and cycle efficiency of the base cycle.
why: A large phase-change cooling effect does not eliminate the work needed to reset the mixture, so parasitic separation losses can erase the cycle's advantage in practice.
key_works: D. Lilley and R. Prasher (2022), *Ionocaloric refrigeration cycle*, DOI:10.1126/science.ade1696.

title: Is a packed plasma catalyst actually catalyzing the surface reaction?
open: When a catalyst packing is inserted into a plasma reactor and yields change, is the surface actually catalyzing the reaction chemically — or is the observed effect merely a consequence of the packing altering discharge geometry, local fields, heating, and plasma composition?
status: Ndayirinde and colleagues found that packed catalysts acted principally as plasma modifiers in their 2023 ammonia experiments (DOI:10.1016/j.cattod.2023.114156). A yield change upon adding a catalyst therefore does not, by itself, establish surface catalysis.
solved_when: An experimental protocol cleanly separates chemical surface catalysis from the physical plasma-modification effects of the packing material, showing whether the surface chemistry contributes beyond those confounding changes.
why: Without this separation, catalyst screening can optimize an electrical packing effect while assigning it the wrong chemical explanation.
key_works: C. Ndayirinde et al. (2023), *Plasma-catalytic ammonia synthesis: Packed catalysts act as plasma modifiers*, DOI:10.1016/j.cattod.2023.114156.

title: Product removal that preserves plasma-synthesis efficiency
open: Can product capture be integrated with plasma-driven ammonia synthesis such that removing product fast enough to suppress back-reaction still yields a net efficiency gain once separation, regeneration, recycle, and pressure losses are counted?
status: Lower product concentration is known to reduce undesired reverse reactions, but it simultaneously creates a harder downstream separation problem; no integrated solution is on record. Key works: Lefferts (2024), plasma-catalysis perspective, DOI:10.1002/ange.202305322.
solved_when: An integrated reaction–separation–regeneration scheme is demonstrated in which lower product concentration suppresses reverse reactions and the complete process (including separation, recycle, and pressure losses) shows a net benefit in energy efficiency over synthesis without product removal.
why: Without this integration, an improved reactor can become a worse complete process — gains in plasma-synthesis efficiency are eaten by downstream separation and regeneration costs.
key_works: Lefferts (2024), plasma-catalysis perspective, DOI:10.1002/ange.202305322.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of the piston model
open: Does the piston energy-exchange process, in the scaling limit, produce the macroscopic heat equation on the scale where Fourier transport is expected? A satisfactory answer should exhibit the limiting equation together with a justified transport coefficient and controlled initial conditions.
status: The 2026 workshop account (Szász, *Fourier law from Hamiltonian dynamics*, discussing the Bálint–Nándori–Szász–Tóth piston-model program) distinguishes obtaining a Markov process in a rare-interaction limit from obtaining its hydrodynamic limit, and explicitly lists the latter as unresolved.
solved_when: The hydrodynamic limit of the piston model is derived as a macroscopic heat equation, with an explicitly identified and justified transport coefficient and controlled initial conditions.
why: A stochastic description of microscopic exchanges is not yet a derivation of Fourier-scale transport; the limit would connect the energy-exchange dynamics to macroscopic heat conduction.
key_works: Szász (2026), *Fourier law from Hamiltonian dynamics*, discussing the Bálint–Nándori–Szász–Tóth piston-model program.

title: Distinguishing wind changes from airborne sensor failure
open: When can measurements from a tethered kite uniquely separate genuine wind changes, aerodynamic changes, and sensor faults, and where this separation is impossible, what is the minimum additional sensing that restores it?
status: Cayon, Watson, and Schmehl (2025) documented cases where sensor saturation or modeling errors produced misleading inferred winds, and showed that constraining an estimated wind component can suppress such artifacts while also hiding real flow.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the conditions under which kite measurements uniquely identify wind, aerodynamic changes, and sensor faults, together with a specification of the minimum additional sensing needed when uniqueness fails.
why: Without this, a controller may respond to an instrument artifact as though it were a gust, acting on nonexistent flow; conversely, suppressing artifacts can hide real wind.
key_works: O. Cayon, S. Watson, and R. Schmehl (2025), *Kite as a sensor: wind and state estimation in tethered flying systems*, DOI:10.5194/wes-10-2161-2025.

title: Closed-loop prediction of suspended control-unit swing
open: Can we predict the coupled motion of a wing and its suspended control unit when aerodynamic forces and steering inputs evolve dynamically, rather than prescribing the measured wing trajectory as a given?
status: Schelbergen and Schmehl's 2024 analysis (DOI:10.5194/wes-9-1323-2024) reproduces important swinging behavior using a two-mass representation, but deliberately excludes parts of the unconstrained aerodynamic and yaw dynamics.
solved_when: A closed-loop model captures the coupled wing and suspended-unit dynamics — including the unconstrained aerodynamic and yaw dynamics — and reproduces the swinging behavior observed in flight.
why: Swinging alters bridle loads, corrupts attitude measurements, and reduces the effectiveness of control actions, so a predictive model is needed to design controllers that account for it.
key_works: M. Schelbergen and R. Schmehl (2024), *Swinging motion of a kite with suspended control unit flying turning manoeuvres*, DOI:10.5194/wes-9-1323-2024.

title: Cycle-to-cycle evolution of recyclable iron-powder morphology
open: Does repeated oxidation–reduction cycling of recyclable iron powder drive particle size, internal porosity, cracks, and phase distribution toward a stable population, or toward progressive fragmentation? A theory or model that predicts the long-time trajectory of the microstructure over many cycles would answer this.
status: Choisez and colleagues resolved major microstructural transformations during iron-powder combustion in 2022 (L. Choisez et al., *Phase transformations and microstructure evolution during combustion of iron powder*, DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2022.118261). Characterizing one transformation does not determine the trajectory of many complete recycling cycles.
solved_when: A predictive account exists for the cycle-to-cycle evolution of particle size, internal porosity, cracking, and phase distribution over many complete recycling cycles, determining whether a stable population or progressive fragmentation results.
why: Reaction rates and collection requirements may change as the fuel is reused, so without such a prediction the practical viability of iron powder as a recyclable fuel remains uncertain.
key_works: L. Choisez et al. (2022), *Phase transformations and microstructure evolution during combustion of iron powder*, DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2022.118261.

title: Mechanism-resolved activation of TiFe hydrogen-storage alloys
open: Which mechanism actually governs the activation of a given TiFe hydrogen-storage alloy — surface oxide conversion, catalytic surface species, secondary phases, or exposure of fresh material through cracking — and can we predict which one dominates from the alloy's preparation and exposure history?
status: TiFe has decades of successful activation methods, but different preparation and exposure histories support different explanations, and no predictive mechanism selection has been achieved; the open problem is mechanism selection, not first activation. Key works: T. Schober (1983), *On the activation of FeTi for hydrogen storage*, DOI:10.1016/0022-5088(83)90249-7; E. M. Dematteis et al. (2021), *Substitutional effects in TiFe for hydrogen storage*, DOI:10.1039/D1MA00101A.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that, given a TiFe sample's preparation and exposure history, correctly identifies the controlling activation mechanism before testing, validated across the distinct activation pathways reported for different preparation routes.
why: Reliable low-temperature commissioning of TiFe-based storage systems requires knowing which mechanism to target, not merely reproducing one preparation recipe.
key_works: T. Schober (1983), *On the activation of FeTi for hydrogen storage*, DOI:10.1016/0022-5088(83)90249-7; E. M. Dematteis et al. (2021), *Substitutional effects in TiFe for hydrogen storage*, DOI:10.1039/D1MA00101A.

title: Testing temperature-dependent coherent phase transformation in palladium hydride
open: Can experiments distinguish a genuine coherent two-phase transformation in palladium hydride from nearly homogeneous hydrogen uptake, as temperature, specimen size, and defect-mediated strain relaxation are varied?
status: Rahm, Löfgren, and Erhart's calculations predict a change in transformation character around 400 K under coherent-system assumptions; real specimens introduce relaxation pathways that must be separated from the predicted effect.
solved_when: Measurements of palladium hydride across varying temperature, specimen size, and defect conditions cleanly separate the coherent two-phase transformation from nearly homogeneous uptake, testing the predicted change in transformation character around 400 K against relaxation effects from real specimens.
why: Hysteresis determines the recoverable work and operating pressures in reversible hydrogen storage, so knowing whether the transformation is coherent or homogeneous directly bears on storage performance.
key_works: J. M. Rahm, J. Löfgren, and P. Erhart (2022), *Quantitative predictions of thermodynamic hysteresis: Temperature-dependent character of the phase transition in Pd–H*, DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2022.117697; arXiv:2110.07883.

title: Desiccants that do not destroy fluoronitrile insulating gas
open: Can water be removed from C₄F₇N/CO₂ insulation systems by a desiccant that neither catalyzes decomposition of the gas nor sheds degradation products of its own? In other: does a desiccant exist that is chemically inert toward the fluoronitrile mixture while doing its drying job?
status: Gao and colleagues' nine-month aging study (W. Gao et al., 2021, *Compatibility of Molecular Sieves with C₄F₇N/CO₂ Insulating Gas Mixture*, DOI:10.1109/CEIDP50766.2021.9705379) found incompatibility for the tested zeolite sieve and possible decomposition of the tested organic alternative; high adsorption area can intensify unwanted chemistry.
solved_when: A desiccant is demonstrated that removes water from the C₄F₇N/CO₂ mixture over the tested aging horizon without measurable gas decomposition and without contamination by desiccant-derived degradation products.
why: A drying component meant to protect the insulation system can instead destroy the insulating medium it serves, so no fluoronitrile-based gas-insulated equipment can be safely dried with current desiccants.
key_works: W. Gao et al. (2021), *Compatibility of Molecular Sieves with C₄F₇N/CO₂ Insulating Gas Mixture*, DOI:10.1109/CEIDP50766.2021.9705379.

title: Spatial validation of HVDC cable aging during polarity reversal
open: Where in the insulation of an HVDC cable does aging actually accumulate when the voltage polarity is reversed, and how do temperature-dependent conductivity and residual trapped charge shape that spatial distribution?
status: Diban and colleagues' 2024 model (B. Diban et al. (2024), *Life Estimation of HVDC Cables Subjected to Fast and Slow Polarity Reversals*, DOI:10.3390/en17133182) predicts strongly nonuniform lifetime reduction, especially in inner insulation; this remains modeled damage distribution, not direct lifetime validation.
solved_when: A spatially resolved experimental validation confirms (or refutes) the predicted location and degree of lifetime reduction across the insulation during fast and slow polarity reversals, including the effects of temperature-dependent conductivity and residual charge.
why: Average electric-field stress can conceal the specific region that governs failure, so design decisions based on aggregate stress may target the wrong location in the insulation.
key_works: B. Diban et al. (2024), *Life Estimation of HVDC Cables Subjected to Fast and Slow Polarity Reversals*, DOI:10.3390/en17133182.

title: Identifiability limits for superconducting inter-tape contact networks
open: Which internal contact resistances in a superconducting inter-tape contact network can be uniquely reconstructed from measurements taken only at the accessible cable terminals, and which contacts are fundamentally unidentifiable without adding further excitations or sensors?
status: The TITO method improves contact-resistance inference by accounting for parallel current paths, but it does not establish arbitrary spatial reconstruction of every internal contact. Key work: R. Teyber et al. (2025), *Tape-in-tape-out: a new approach for in-situ contact resistance measurements in high temperature superconducting CORC cables*, DOI:10.1088/1361-6668/aded3b.
solved_when: A complete classification exists that identifies, for a given network and measurement configuration, exactly which internal contact resistances are uniquely determined by terminal data and which are not, together with conditions under which additional excitations or sensors restore uniqueness.
why: Without such a classification, a terminal measurement risks being overinterpreted as a unique internal defect map, mislocating or spuriously identifying defects inside the cable.
key_works: R. Teyber et al. (2025), *Tape-in-tape-out: a new approach for in-situ contact resistance measurements in high temperature superconducting CORC cables*, DOI:10.1088/1361-6668/aded3b.

title: Whole-system energy advantage of conduction-cooled flux pumps
open: When, if ever, does a contactless flux pump actually save electricity for the whole magnet system once every hidden cost is counted? Formally: determine the conditions under which flux pumping reduces total energy consumption relative to conventional current leads, with alternating-field losses, cryocooler work, switching losses, and avoided current-lead heat loads all included in the accounting.
status: Iftikhar and colleagues (2025, *A compact conduction cooled flux pump operating below 77 K*, DOI:10.1088/1361-6668/adaf5c) demonstrated conduction-cooled flux pumping below 77 K, but successful current injection does not by itself identify the most efficient operating temperature and excitation schedule.
solved_when: A quantitative criterion or model identifies the operating temperature and excitation schedule at which conduction-cooled flux pumping minimizes whole-system electricity consumption, showing when the avoided current-lead heat load outweighs the added alternating-field, cryocooler, and switching burdens.
why: Removing a warm-to-cold conductor looks like a pure gain, but it can simply relocate the energy cost into other refrigeration burdens, so system designers currently have no way to know whether flux pumping is a net win.
key_works: M. H. Iftikhar et al. (2025), *A compact conduction cooled flux pump operating below 77 K*, DOI:10.1088/1361-6668/adaf5c.

title: Radical-pathway selectivity during electrocatalytic heat release
open: Can a low-voltage electrocatalytic trigger convert quadricyclane back to norbornadiene without simultaneously unlocking irreversible side reactions of the post-electron-transfer radical species, especially where the relevant electronic states demand a multireference description? The challenge is to predict and control the branching between the desired energy-releasing pathway and destructive follow-up chemistry, including states inadequately captured by a single reference configuration.
status: Franz and colleagues show strong substituent dependence and explicitly identify more advanced electronic-structure treatment as a remaining need.
solved_when: A theory exists that quantitatively predicts which substituents and electrocatalytic conditions steer the radical intermediates selectively toward quadricyclane-to-norbornadiene conversion rather than irreversible pathways, validly treating the multireference electronic states involved.
why: Low triggering voltage alone is insufficient if it opens destructive reaction pathways; without such selectivity, the stored solar energy of a molecular solar thermal system is lost to parasitic chemistry rather than released on demand.
key_works: E. Franz et al. (2025), *Tuning Electrocatalytic Energy Release in Norbornadiene Based Molecular Solar Thermal Systems Through Substituent Effects*, DOI:10.1002/chem.202502294.

title: Unambiguous rarefaction-shock identification in dense organic vapor
open: Can a finite-amplitude rarefaction shock be observed in a dense organic vapor in a way that unambiguously rules out ordinary explanations — temperature inhomogeneity, fluid decomposition, and measurement artifacts — while verifying the thermodynamic states required for its nonclassical interpretation?
status: The 2025 ASTER experiments (C. Medipali et al., *Rarefaction Shockwave Experiments in Dense Organic Vapours*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-92695-2_16) report repeatable departures from classical gas dynamics near the working fluid's thermal-stability limit; such departures do not, by themselves, uniquely identify a rarefaction shock. Related nonclassical wave-propagation measurements appear in N. Chandrasekaran et al. (2024), DOI:10.1007/s00348-024-03843-8.
solved_when: A repeatable experimental observation of a finite-amplitude rarefaction shock near the working fluid's thermal-stability limit is reported, with independent exclusion of temperature inhomogeneity, fluid decomposition, and measurement artifacts, and with the thermodynamic states required for the nonclassical interpretation verified.
why: It would test a distinctive prediction of nonconvex-fluid thermodynamics that bears directly on the design of machinery operating with dense vapors.
key_works: C. Medipati et al. (2025), *Rarefaction Shockwave Experiments in Dense Organic Vapours*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-92695-2_16; N. Chandrasekaran et al. (2024), *Nonclassical wave propagation measurements in the high temperature vapor of D6…*, DOI:10.1007/s00348-024-03843-8.

title: Magnetic damping of bidirectional metal-pad waves
open: Can magnetic damping be measured for interfacial waves that vary in both horizontal directions, with the complex induced-current patterns resolved directly rather than extrapolated from one-dimensional modes?
status: Hegde and colleagues validate magnetic damping only for the particular mode \(m=1,n=0\); bidirectional-mode validation is explicitly outstanding (Hegde, Herreman, and Horstmann (2025), *Stability theory for metal pad roll with consideration of viscous and magnetic damping*, arXiv:2507.18301).
solved_when: An experiment (or equivalent measurement) quantifies magnetic damping of bidirectional interfacial modes, resolving the induced-current patterns, thereby extending validation beyond the one-dimensional mode \(m=1,n=0\).
why: These modes participate in instabilities of conducting liquid layers, so their damping behavior is needed to predict and control such instabilities rather than infer them from one-dimensional extrapolations.
key_works: Hegde, Herreman, and Horstmann (2025), *Stability theory for metal pad roll with consideration of viscous and magnetic damping*, arXiv:2507.18301.

title: Cold-electron control of mirror-expander heat losses
open: Predict the self-consistent potential and heat transport in a mirror expander when cold electrons are supplied at the boundary by secondary emission and local ionization. That is, solve for the sheath/presheath structure and upstream energy flux with these electron sources included self-consistently.
status: The studied model, in Tyushev et al. (2025), *Drift-kinetic PIC simulations of plasma flow and energy transport in the magnetic mirror configuration* (arXiv:2501.15604), omits these electron sources; they are identified as relevant extensions, since a collisionless injected distribution does not represent every operating boundary.
solved_when: A model or simulation that incorporates secondary-emission and ionization-produced cold electrons yields a self-consistent potential profile and heat-transport prediction in the expander, valid across operating boundaries not captured by a purely collisionless injected distribution.
why: Boundary-created cold-electron populations can alter upstream confinement and exhaust power, so without them expander models may mispredict the power exhaust of mirror devices.
key_works: Tyushev et al. (2025), *Drift-kinetic PIC simulations of plasma flow and energy transport in the magnetic mirror configuration*, arXiv:2501.15604.

title: Charge-selective trapping with nonthermal ion mixtures
open: Can centrifugal confinement traps selectively trap ions when the ion mixture is beam-like rather than Maxwellian, and can that selectivity be predicted and sustained in a full kinetic operating model — including the power needed to maintain the nonthermal distribution?
status: The ion-mixture study of Kolmes, Ochs, and Fisch (2025), *Ion Mix Can Invert Centrifugal Traps* (arXiv:2504.18634) identifies qualitatively different selection possibilities for nonthermal populations, but no complete kinetic operating model exists.
solved_when: A kinetic model predicts which ion species are retained or expelled for a specified beam-like (non-Maxwellian) mixture, reproduces the qualitative selection possibilities already identified for nonthermal populations, and quantifies the power required to sustain those distributions against relaxation.
why: It determines whether deliberately maintaining nonthermal ion distributions can invert or retune which species a centrifugal trap keeps or expels, and at what energetic cost — turning a qualitative observation into a designable species-separation capability.
key_works: Kolmes, Ochs, and Fisch (2025), *Ion Mix Can Invert Centrifugal Traps*, arXiv:2504.18634.

title: Suppressing alpha-induced neutron side reactions without sacrificing heating
open: Can fast alphas in a proton–boron-11 plasma be kept away from boron in energy or phase space, so that alpha-induced neutron-producing side reactions are suppressed, while the alphas still deposit enough of their energy to heat the plasma usefully?
status: A 2025 ash study (Ochs, Kolmes, and Fisch, *Preventing ash from poisoning proton-boron 11 fusion plasmas*, DOI:10.1063/5.0266369) distinguishes thermal-ash control from neutron-producing reactions involving fast alphas, showing that removing already thermalized helium does not solve the separate fast-alpha problem.
solved_when: A scheme is specified in which the energetic-alpha–boron overlap is demonstrably reduced while maintaining sufficient useful alpha-energy transfer to the plasma, with the tradeoff quantified.
why: Even with an "aneutronic" primary fuel, fast alphas driving neutron-producing side reactions remain a real neutron source, so suppressing them is what would actually deliver low-neutron operation.
key_works: Ochs, Kolmes, and Fisch (2025), *Preventing ash from poisoning proton-boron 11 fusion plasmas*, DOI:10.1063/5.0266369.

title: Identity of the intermediate state in lead zirconate
open: When lead zirconate passes through its narrow intermediate regime, is that regime a genuine equilibrium phase of its own, a coexistence mixture of neighboring phases, or a structure merely trapped by kinetics? A sharper formulation asks for the conditions under which each interpretation applies.
status: Zhang and colleagues' 2024 deep-learning interatomic potential simulations (arXiv:2406.09011) reproduce the major thermal behavior of PbZrO₃ but not every reported intermediate state; the interpretation of the intermediate regime remains dependent on conditions and modeling.
solved_when: The intermediate regime in PbZrO₃ is definitively identified as a distinct equilibrium phase, a mixture, or a kinetically retained structure, with the assignment shown to be valid across the relevant ranges of conditions and modeling assumptions.
why: The phase identity of the intermediate state determines how switching pathways in PbZrO₃ should be modeled.
key_works: H. Zhang et al. (2024), *Finite-temperature properties of antiferroelectric perovskite PbZrO3 from deep learning interatomic potential*, arXiv:2406.09011.

title: Microstructure-to-knee prediction through percolation
open: Can we predict, from measurable microstructural quantities alone, when an electrode's gradual degradation — pore blockage, loss of contact, or damage to the conductive network — will trigger a sharp transition ("knee") in performance? A complete answer would give a quantitative, microstructure-based prediction of the knee point, rather than fitting knee locations to aging data after the fact.
status: Percolation and threshold mechanisms are recognized explanations for knees in aging trajectories (Attia et al. 2022, *"Knees" in lithium-ion battery aging trajectories*, arXiv:2201.02891), but quantitative prediction of knees across realistic evolving electrode networks remains incomplete.
solved_when: A theory or model maps measurable microstructure features of an evolving electrode network to the onset and location of a knee, with quantitative predictions validated across realistic degradation trajectories and not reliant on fitted knee locations.
why: It would connect abrupt macroscopic aging behavior to microscopic design features that engineers can actually control, turning knee avoidance from an empirical observation into a design objective.
key_works: Attia et al. (2022), *“Knees” in lithium-ion battery aging trajectories*, arXiv:2201.02891.

title: Thousand-cycle durability of immobilized protein separators
open: Can an immobilized protein separator survive a full industrial service life? The target is a proposed 1,000 capture–release cycles with at least 90% retained useful separation performance, tested under realistic contaminants and regeneration conditions rather than benign laboratory cycling.
status: Ye and colleagues (2025, *Group Separation of Rare Earth Elements by Protein-Functionalized Magnetic Nanoparticles*, DOI:10.1021/acsestengg.5c00508) demonstrated protein-functionalized magnetic particles retaining more than 90% activity over five studied cycles — proof of reuse, but not evidence for the proposed thousand-cycle lifetime target.
